t: Aramaic, first written by the Aramaean kingdoms of Syria in the 9th century BCE, became the common language of the Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian empires, used from Egypt to the borders of India.
It was the everyday language of Jesus and of the Jews of his time, the language of parts of the Bible and most of the Talmud, and, as Syriac, of one of the great literatures of Eastern Christianity.

Its alphabet is the ancestor of the Hebrew, Arabic and Syriac scripts and of many others in Asia, and its modern forms are still spoken by Assyrian, Chaldean, Syriac, Jewish and Mandaean communities, though they are endangered.
dyk: In the Syrian village of Maaloula and two villages nearby, people still speak Western Neo-Aramaic, the last living form of the western branch of Aramaic, to which the dialect of Jesus’ Galilee belonged.
ev: A statue at Tell Fekheriye in Syria carries one of the oldest Aramaic inscriptions, beside an Akkadian text
The Assyrian empire uses Aramaic beside Akkadian, spreading it across the Near East
Papyri of the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt record the Aramaic of the Persian empire
The Indian emperor Ashoka has an edict inscribed in Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar
Jesus and his disciples speak Aramaic in Galilee
The Babylonian Talmud, written largely in Aramaic, takes shape
After the Arab conquests, Arabic begins to replace Aramaic across the Near East
The advance of the Islamic State drives Aramaic-speaking Christians from their towns in northern Iraq

f.family: Afroasiatic: the Northwest Semitic branch, close to Hebrew and Phoenician
f.script: The Aramaic alphabet, derived from the Phoenician; its descendants include the Hebrew square script, Syriac, Nabataean (the ancestor of Arabic script) and many scripts of Central and South Asia
f.earliest: Inscriptions of the Aramaean kingdoms of Syria from the 9th century BCE, such as the statue of Tell Fekheriye
f.status: Spoken today in its modern forms by several hundred thousand people, many of them in diaspora communities; Syriac is used in the liturgy of several churches
